title: Whale survey
titleCn: 鲸鱼调查表设计（海洋生物船旅准备）

paragraphs.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-seven.
What exactly have we got to do for next week's marine biology boat trip? I missed the meeting.
Um, we've got to do some preparation for the marine mammal survey.
Uh-huh.
While we're at sea, we'll be looking particularly for whales and identifying any we see from the boat, and we've got to prepare a survey framework to use.
You mean decide on the headings for a table, that sort of thing?
Exactly. So I'll write it down as we're going along, shall I?
Okay.
Main heading,
whale survey.
Um, what next? We need all the headings, starting with the general information ones. What do you think the first one should be?
Well, date. We better start with that.
Mm-hmm.
And then after that, watch times. That's pretty standard on all survey reports.
Mm, okay. Then I think it'll be important to record what the sea's like at the time. You know, whether it's calm, whether it's choppy or whatever.
Yes, put that. Uh, and then the weather too.
Uh, the next section should be for recording what it's like.
Okay.
Anything else about the general conditions? Oh, I know, visibility.
It'll have to be an estimate, of course.
Shall we say to the nearest fifty meters?
I think that's too exact. A hundred would be more realistic.
Right.
And yes, one other thing. We should record whether there are any fishing boats. That's useful information to get.
Right.
Then we need details about the actual whale sightings. So what do we need there?
Well, I'm not sure how we should put this, but you'd need to know where the whale was, wouldn't you? I mean, exactly what the ship's position was at the time.
Okay. Let's call it location. That would cover it, wouldn't it?
How are you supposed to know that, by the way?
There's an electronic chart on one of the decks. You have to get someone else to run and check for you.
Oh, okay.
Mm.
Um,
I'd say the next heading should be description.
Mm, don't you think that's a bit vague?
Mm.
Shouldn't we have more specific subheadings to go with it? Something like size or shape or color or-
Well, I, I think just two would do. First, appearance. People could just note down any aspect that they feel certain about.
Okay. And the second one?
That could just be behavior, and that should cover everything. If you make the headings too specific, people start making guesses even when they're not really sure.
Yes, you're probably right.
Then we should have a section on whether seabirds are present too, because that can be quite important.
Yes, but
wait a minute. Before that, we should have one for recording the size of the group in case there's more than one whale.
Mm.
And another section for recording the presence of any young ones with them.
Okay, but juveniles is the specialist term. Let's put that.
Mm-hmm.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-eight to thirty.
Now listen and answer questions twenty-eight to thirty.
We've got to identify the whales in these drawings. Look.
Oh, okay. I suppose size is the most obvious thing that distinguishes them.
Well, size or shape,
or whether there's a dorsal fin on the top of its back.
Don't they all have fins on their backs? I mean, how do they stabilize without one?
Well, I don't know, but look, neither of these has one.
Oh, yes.
This one's just got small bumps along its back, but it doesn't actually have a fin.
Yes. I think that's a sperm whale.
Oh.
Oh, and the other one without a fin is a northern right whale.
How do you know?
From the shape of its flippers. They've got this distinctive paddle shape. See? They're square at the ends.
Oh, right. Yes. Uh, good. That's two we've got.
Okay, good.
And the biggest one's the blue whale.
It looks just like this other one here.
That's right. But this other one's only about a quarter of the size of the blue whale. It's a minke whale. I saw one of those once.
Well, we're doing quite well.
Oh, yes, definitely. Good work. Now all we have to do is to-
